I'm curious as well as partially conflicted right now.

At this moment, I am working on a news website. The desktop site uses thumbnail images alongside a brief article caption. Since it's on the desktop site, it looks nice and plays well, especially since you expect slightly better internet performance for desktop users. Now, for my mobile optimized, I am trying to consider if I should remove those images from displaying, or figure out a way to bring them in the same way it is on the desktop site.

I've already removed them, but the mobile site looks extremely bare without them now... What should I do? What are some alternative options I may be able to turn to? Any ideas?
Images or no images for mobile version of news site... I'm conflicted, help!
I have a phone with a large screen (Galaxy Note 3) and even with that sometimes images annoy me. Perhaps a "display images" toggle at the top of the page that saves state between visits on a device?
Yeah, I could look into that. I think I may have to add another way to help identify what each article is about another way of images were to be disabled.

I'm assuming these are large images, otherwise it probably wouldn't be a performance problem. If they are in fact large images, you could save mobile-friendly versions of the image and use CSS media queries to display the mobile-optimized versions, and respectively the desktop versions.

The mobile optimized versions should be 768px in width or less, and display on screens with a CSS max-width of 767px. Then the desktop versions would be displayed on screens with a CSS min-width of 768px. You could structure your media queries differently (e.g. "mobile first"), this is just an example.

This is pretty much what I have been doing. Basically for every full-sized image I have been creating a thumbnail version of it to display.

At the moment I decided to go with a Title only version for mobile users, while Tablet/PC users will get thumbnail images and titles.
$1 billion lawsuit: Beleaguered Haggen sues Albertsons for undermining its rollout

While it might indeed be the case that Albertsons used some sneaky business to harm Haggen, it could also just be a failed rollout. Rather than admit they screwed it up, of course Haggen wants to bring in the lawyers. How could anyone look at buying a supermarket chain in southern California and not realize the type of competition and customer loyalty they would face? When the local Albertsons changed its name to Haggen, people simply stopped shopping there. Because what the hell is a Haggen?
That explains all the shifting coupon tactics.

Going from 18 to 162 stores overnight is going to bring severe problems.

But, blaming their pricing decisions on "what Albertson's told them" is ridiculous horsecrap.

I worked as a floor manager and later an executive for a small, independent 6 store supermarket chain, and we had a person whose sole job was traveling to competitor's stores and checking pricing. Each morning, the app would grab 200-250 items, print out a worksheet with current pricing and a place for competitor prices, and the person would go to stores and write them down. Everyone does it.

We would have Kroger employees come to our stores to do it. They would be all embarrassed about it, so we would go find them, chit-chat, offer to help them find items to make their jobs easier, etc.

So when one of the biggest issues in their failed rollout was "Albertson's told us the prices to use, and we didn't know any better", it's their own damn fault for not doing even a whit of research or validation or due diligence. Sorry, not sorry.
